entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Georgetown University in Washington, D.C., founded 1789 by Bishop John Carroll as the first Catholic and Jesuit university in the United States — established in the same year as the US Constitution's ratification — is the oldest Catholic university in America and the most politically connected university in the world, given its location 3 km from the US Capitol. Georgetown produces more foreign leaders (presidents, prime ministers) as alumni than any other American university; its School of Foreign Service (1919) is consistently ranked the world's top school of international affairs.

John Carroll's 1789 founding was deliberate: the Jesuit educator who had supported the American Revolution chose Georgetown's location — above the Potomac, near the new federal capital — specifically to create a Catholic institution that would demonstrate Catholic citizens' loyalty to the new republic. Georgetown became the training ground for generations of Catholic public figures, senators, ambassadors, and presidents.

Georgetown's School of Foreign Service (1919) — the world's oldest school of international affairs — was founded in response to World War I to train Americans for the new international role the US was assuming. SFS alumni include Bill Clinton, King Felipe VI of Spain, King Abdullah II of Jordan, and dozens of prime ministers and foreign ministers. Georgetown's location creates an unusual academic-political symbiosis: think tanks, government officials, and Georgetown professors regularly interchange roles. The university's 1838 sale of 272 enslaved people (GU272) to pay off debts is among the most documented instances of a university's direct participation in the domestic slave trade.
